title: Teaching without preaching
hook: Epictetus points at sheep: they don't show the shepherd their grass, they grow wool
tomorrow: why did a king's sleepless night save Mordecai?

segments.voice: The ordinary days ended in Yan Hui's narrow lane: plain and good. Now the last stretch of living it begins, and it's about passing it on.

Somebody takes up cold plunges, or a budgeting app, and now every dinner turns into a seminar on it. Even when they're right, you start dreading the subject. Epictetus, a Stoic teacher, had a picture for this, and it's sheep. In his Handbook, he points at a flock in a field. Sheep, he says, don't bring up their grass to show the shepherd how much they've eaten. So what do they show?
screen: `EVERY DINNER, A SEMINAR.` → `EPICTETUS POINTS AT SHEEP.` → `THEY DON'T SHOW THE GRASS.`

segments.voice: They digest it, and what shows is wool and milk. So, Epictetus says, don't show people your principles. Show them what your principles have grown. Never call yourself a philosopher. At a dinner, don't explain how one ought to eat; eat as one ought. When talk turns to big ideas among people who haven't asked, mostly keep quiet. Then a story about Socrates. People would come to him and ask to be introduced to some philosophers, and Socrates would take them along to meet others. He didn't mind being overlooked. That's the Stoic teaching: the proof is the life, and the life is quiet about itself. Matthew's Gospel has a line close to this, in its own words. There, Jesus warns about false prophets and says: "Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them." Fruit and wool: what a life produces is what tells. And an honest difference. Matthew's Gospel ends with Jesus sending his followers out: "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations." There, speaking is part of the call. Epictetus asks for quiet; the Gospel sends people out to speak. Two different callings, and both trust that the words have to be backed by a life.
screen: `SHOW WHAT YOUR PRINCIPLES GREW.` · `SOCRATES, HAPPY TO BE OVERLOOKED.` · `BY THEIR FRUITS YE SHALL KNOW THEM.` · `ONE ASKS FOR QUIET, ONE SENDS OUT.` · then, large: `SHOW THE WOOL.`

segments.voice: Sit the way you would if someone could see you and you had nothing to explain: upright, easy, hands still in your lap. Let your face soften. For the rest of the sit, let the posture be the whole message.
Teaching without preaching: passing on a way of life by living it where others can see, and saying little about it unless they ask.
Carry this: show the wool, and let it do the talking, the way the flock does. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Stoic readers take Epictetus at his word: they practice where others can see, don't call themselves philosophers, and say little about principles unless asked.

chat.meaning: Epictetus said sheep don't bring up grass to show what they ate; they grow wool. Show what your principles produce, not the principles.
